item.content:encoded:
I love using AI as a writing tool. But like I wrote in “Why Does AI Write Like Yoda?,” it’s not because AI is a good writer. In fact, it’s pretty bad at writing, and I edit absolutely everything it generates, so the end result is basically unrecognizable compared to what it created. Unfortunately, just because AI is, on average, a pretty lousy writer, that doesn’t stop people from using AI to write all sorts of things that people end up reading, and that’s how we end up with slop.

That’s where watermarking comes in. If AI-written text carries a hidden signal that a machine can pick up, someone could build slop filters with it and add a little friction to mass-producing AI text and stuffing it into every nook and cranny of the internet and, maybe, manage to keep some spaces on the internet for people. (Anthropic and OpenAI give a more official reason: the EU AI Act now requires them to mark AI-generated content in a way machines can read. I don’t know how they feel about slop.)

The upshot is that almost everything Claude writes now carries a hidden watermark. A slop filter needs a way to check for the watermark. And, unfortunately, for the time being, only the big AI companies and a few organizations they’ve approved can check for it.

Anthropic’s support page on marking AI-generated content now reports all of its newest models, and some older ones, watermark their text on every surface where you can use Claude, worldwide. (Bruce Hopkins covered what Anthropic announced here on Radar.) Google has used a text watermark in its Gemini app since 2024, and in October OpenAI announced it’s adding one to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU. But none of those companies lets the public check text with its detector. (Google’s synthid.com lets anyone check images, video, and audio for its watermark, including images made with ChatGPT, but it won’t let you check text from any AI lab.)

I’ve read articles about watermarking, but I didn’t really know much about how it worked. So I did what any good developer would probably do: I took a shot at reasoning about it, and I came up with what I thought was a plausible way watermarking could work, based on what I know about how large language models work. And, strangely enough, it turned out I was basically right, and not because I’m some sort of amazing genius. It’s because watermarking is actually pretty straightforward, and if you know how the output part of an LLM works, you can probably design a decent watermarking system yourself.

The reason I’ve got such a big interest in how models work right now is my next O’Reilly book, a deep dive into how models work called Be the Model, which we’re planning on releasing early next year. I’ve spent a lot of time over the last year thinking really hard about how to explain the internals of LLMs, and it turns out that you don’t need to understand most of the parts inside a model to see how watermarking works. All you need is the very tail end.

So let’s try an experiment. I’m going to describe the relevant bits of how models work, and then, before I explain how watermarking works, I want you to take a guess and see how close you come.

The only part of the model you need

There’s a lot of stuff that happens inside a model. You’ve probably heard of transformer blocks, and you might know what a context window is. That’s all part of the whole machine. But at its core, a model is a next-word-predicting machine: You feed it a bunch of text as context, and it predicts the next word. The part that matters for watermarking is what goes into that machine and what comes out.

What goes into the machine is tokens. We all know that when you pay an API bill, you pay some number of dollars per million tokens, but we don’t always explain what a token is. Remember when people discovered that AIs were really bad at counting the r’s in the word strawberry? Part of the reason for that is that the AI never sees letters. It only works with numbers.

Every model has a fixed vocabulary of tokens, which are every word and piece of word it knows, and each token has a number called its token ID. On the way into the machine, a tokenizer splits your text into tokens and replaces each one with its ID. For example, if you ask GPT-2 (an early LLM created by OpenAI in 2019) “how many r’s are in strawberry,” its tokenizer turns the word strawberry into a single token, number 41236. The model gets that number, not the letters s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y, so it doesn’t have any actual letters to count.

Common words usually get a token of their own. But a word that isn’t in the vocabulary gets split into smaller pieces that are, which is how a tokenizer can handle any text you give it. GPT-2’s vocabulary has a token for "strawberry" with a space in front of it, but not for "strawberry" without the space. So if strawberry is the very first word of the text, with no space in front of it, the tokenizer splits it into three pieces that are in the vocabulary: st, raw, and berry.

GPT-2 has 50,257 tokens in its vocabulary. If you have Python and install the Hugging Face transformers library, you can check GPT-2’s vocabulary size and strawberry tokens with this command:

python3 -c "from transformers import AutoTokenizer; 
t=AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2'); print(len(t)); 
print(t.tokenize(' strawberry'), t.tokenize('strawberry'))"

If you don’t have Python or don’t feel like installing transformers, you can go to ChatGPT, Claude.ai, or Gemini and paste that command in, and they’ll (probably) install the library and run it for you. It should print 50257, then ['Ġstrawberry'] ['st', 'raw', 'berry']. The Ġ is how this tokenizer writes the space. (If you don’t have PyTorch installed, you’ll see a warning about it first, which you can ignore.)

The token IDs go into the context window, which is just a big array of numbers, and then the AI does its thing. The context window contains every token the model sees when it’s making its next-word prediction. If you’re using a chat, it usually includes the whole conversation so far (your earlier prompts and the AI’s earlier responses) plus any instructions or files the chat app adds behind the scenes. When you send a new message, it typically gets added to the end of the context window, as does every token the AI writes in reply, so the window keeps growing as the conversation goes on (up to a size limit, at which point the app has to compact or drop older parts of it).

What comes out the other end of the machine is a probability for every token in the entire vocabulary: the model’s estimate of how likely each one is to be the next token, with all of them adding up to 100%.

The model’s job ends at the probabilities, and it never picks a word. Picking the next token is the job of a separate program called the inference runtime, or runner. The runner can take the most likely token every time, or it can roll the dice and pick a token at random, giving each one a chance that matches its probability. We’re used to thinking of AI as nondeterministic: give the same AI the exact same prompt 10 times in a row and you’ll get 10 slightly different answers, sometimes wildly different answers. That randomness is all done in the runner. Give the model the same context window and it produces the same probabilities. Then the runner adds the token it picked to the context window and runs the model again to get the next one.

Can you guess how a simple watermark works?

If you wanted to hide a pattern in an AI’s text that you could detect later, and all you could touch was the probabilities or the runner’s dice roll, how would you do it?

Here’s what I guessed. I’d divide the tokens into two groups, then I’d nudge up the probabilities for one group and nudge down the probabilities for the other. Then, since I’d know which tokens are in the favored group, I could do some pretty basic statistical analysis to figure out whether they show up more often than they should, and if they do, the text is probably watermarked.

That turns out to be a real, well-known watermark called the green list method, from a 2023 paper by John Kirchenbauer and his colleagues at the University of Maryland, “A Watermark for Large Language Models.” They called the favored group a green list, and the rest of the vocabulary a red list. Right before it picks, the runner gives every green token’s probability a boost. The red tokens never get touched, but each one’s share goes down, because the probabilities still have to add up to 100%.

Here’s an example. Say a tiny model only knows five words (cat, tree, the, by, and sat), and it has just read the word the, so it’s predicting the next word. The first probability column shows the probability the model gives each of its five words. Now say tree and by are on the green list for this spot, so the runner boosts those two before it picks. The second probability column shows the probabilities after the boost:

Tree is now tied with cat. The model produced the same probabilities as before, and the runner boosted two of them after the model was done.

My guess missed an important detail, though. The green list can’t be the same every time the runner picks a token. If it were, the same favored words would show up all over the text, and anyone who read enough of it could work out which ones they were. So the runner determines the green list for each token using a secret key mixed with the token right before it. To check for the watermark, take each token in the text, use the key and the previous token to rebuild its green list, and check whether the token is on it. If the green list is half the vocabulary, you’d expect about half the tokens in ordinary text to be green by chance. In watermarked text, a lot more of them are green. A statistical test tells you how unlikely it would be to get that many green tokens by chance. You don’t need the model to check, just the key and the tokenizer.

SynthID: What Claude actually uses

Anthropic says Claude’s watermark is a version of SynthID-Text, a method Google DeepMind published in Nature in 2024 and uses in its own Gemini app. It works in the runner, just like the green list, but it gets the pattern into the text a different way. Anthropic describes it as a watermark that “only changes the source of the randomness used to pick among words.” So my guess was a real method, but Claude uses a different one.

Here’s the basic idea. Instead of boosting some words’ probabilities, the runner rolls its dice a few times, so it ends up with a few candidates for the next word. Then it flips a coin for each candidate. Whether the coin comes up heads or tails depends on the secret key, the candidate word, and the few words right before it, so anyone with the key can flip the same coin later and get the same result. The runner writes a candidate whose coin came up heads. If every candidate is the same word, there’s nothing to choose between, so the watermark only gets into the spots where the model had a real choice.

To check a text, a detector with the key goes through it word by word, redoes each coin flip, and counts the heads. Ordinary text comes up heads about half the time, and watermarked text comes up heads more often. The real detectors do more than count, but that’s the idea.

That’s kind of involved and hard to picture from a description alone. Luckily, I’ve got a better way for you to understand how watermarking works.

Be the Watermark

I mentioned that my new book, Be the Model, will be out next year. It starts from the fact that AI tools have gotten incredibly sophisticated, even the web chats like ChatGPT and Claude.ai. They can run Python code for you, and they can write an entire interactive HTML page from a single prompt. So why not use them as learning tools?

That’s one of the main ideas behind the book. You’ll use AI tools to create web pages (which I call “toys”) that let you play with different parts of LLMs, and that helps you get an intuitive feel for how they work. The toys let you literally do part of the job that a model does, so you learn how a model works by being the model.

Each toy starts with a short prompt and a picture of what the page should look like. I figured that for this article, you could build a toy to Be the Watermark. I think this is actually a good way to get a feel for how SynthID actually works.

Save the picture below, then copy the prompt under it, and paste them both into a fresh ChatGPT or Claude.ai chat. (In the book, you aren’t handed canned prompts; you come up with most of them yourself.)

Once the AI finishes building it, you’ll have a page with a short story and a secret key, 3 1 4 1 5. Most of the words in the story have a dropdown with near-equivalent words, like creek, pond, lake, and pool. Click Run, and the page checks the story the same way a detector does. It goes through the story one word at a time and flips each word’s coin. To flip the coin, it multiplies the token IDs of that word and the four before it by the five key digits, adds them up, and calls it heads if the last digit is 5 through 9. (In the toy, a word’s token ID is just its position in an alphabetical list of every word on the page.) In the picture, the page is checking creek. The five words tabby, rested, by, the, and creek have token IDs 62, 48, 8, 63, and 11. Multiplied by the key digits 3, 1, 4, 1, and 5, that’s 186 + 48 + 32 + 63 + 55 = 384, and the last digit is 4, so creek comes up tails. Then the page counts the heads. The starting story comes up heads on 14 of its 32 coin flips, which is about half, so the page shows “No watermark found.”

Paste this four-paragraph prompt along with the picture into your favorite AI (it works great with ChatGPT):

Build one HTML page with a white background that works like the attached picture. Make all of the text, including the button labels and the key digits, a dark color with high contrast against its background. A word’s token ID is its position, counting from 0, in an alphabetical list of every different word in the story and the dropdowns. Ignore case and punctuation.

The story starts: On a sunny day, the tabby rested by the creek. A duck glided over the water. The dog ran to the beach and barked. The toad jumped onto a rock. The bird sang in the tree.

Each word after the first four that’s in one of these groups gets a dropdown with its group: cat/kitten/kitty/tabby, sat/rested/waited/stayed, by/beside/near, pond/lake/pool/creek, duck/goose/swan, swam/paddled/floated/drifted/glided, across/over, dog/puppy/hound/pup, ran/raced/dashed/hurried/rushed, to/toward, shore/bank/beach, barked/yapped/growled/howled, frog/toad, jumped/hopped/leaped/sprang, onto/upon, rock/stone/log, bird/robin/sparrow/wren, sang/chirped/tweeted/whistled, in/from, tree/oak/elm/maple. In an open dropdown, every option shows whether its coin comes up heads or tails in that spot with the current key; a closed dropdown shows just the word.

The coin flip is the sum in the picture: the key digits times the token IDs of the four words before and the word itself. If the sum’s last digit is 5 to 9, it’s heads; 0 to 4 is tails. Check the story one word at a time, starting with the fifth word, animating each product and the growing sum, highlighting the word and the four before it, and counting the heads. A full run takes about 10 seconds. When the check finishes with at least 60% heads, animate a checkmark badge reading “Watermark detected” beside the heads count; otherwise show “No watermark found.” Changing the key or a word clears the heads count. Use only Step, Run, and Reset buttons. Reset keeps the key and the words.

Your job is to be the watermark. When you open a dropdown, it shows whether each word in it would come up heads or tails in that spot with the current key. Swap some tails words for heads words and run the check again. When at least 60% of the coin flips come up heads (20 of the 32), the page shows a “Watermark detected” badge. Every time you pick a heads word from a dropdown, you’re doing the runner’s job. The one difference is that the runner can only choose among the few candidates its dice rolls turned up, so sometimes there are no heads word to pick.

It’s a little harder than it seems because when you swap one word, it changes the coin flips for the next four words too. Each word’s coin flip uses that word and the four words before it, so the word you just swapped is part of the next four sums, and any of those coin flips can come out differently. A few things to know:

  • A swap never changes the coin flips for words before it, so it helps to work from left to right, the same way the runner writes.
  • A swap can cost you a heads on a word that doesn’t have a dropdown, like the or water. The only way to fix one of those is to change a word before it.
  • If you go back and change an earlier word, some of the words you already picked might now come up differently, so check the dropdowns again.

See if you can get the page to show a watermark for your story.

Once you get the badge, change the last digit of the key to 6 and run the check again. Your heads count will probably drop back toward half and the watermark badge will disappear, even though the watermark is still there, because the page is checking with the wrong key. (A story can still pass with the wrong key by chance.)

You’ll also notice that the first four words, “On a sunny day,” don’t have dropdowns, and the check doesn’t start until the fifth word. A coin flip needs a word and the four words before it, so the first four words don’t have enough words before them to flip a coin.

If you want to see the math for a particular word, ask the AI that built the page how it calculated whether that word comes up heads or tails. It should walk you through the token IDs, the key digits, and the sum. And if the animation feels slow, you can ask it to redo the page so the animation runs faster. To get the original story back, reload the page.

The toy’s vocabulary has 75 words, and 48 of them, like pool and puppy, don’t show up in the starting story. They’re the near-equivalent words in the dropdowns. A real model’s vocabulary works the same way because it’s fixed ahead of time and any one passage uses only a small part of it.

A story this short also shows why real detectors work better on longer text. With 32 fair coin flips that don’t affect each other, you’d get at least 60% heads about one time in 9, so a badge on a story this short doesn’t prove much. Over hundreds of words, the odds of that proportion of heads by chance get very small.

The toy is a lot simpler than the real thing. Real token IDs aren’t alphabetical. Real SynthID uses a much bigger key, mixes the key and the words together with a hash function instead of a sum, and plays several rounds of coin flips for every word instead of one. And its detectors weigh those rounds differently and are trained on watermarked and ordinary text for each key, instead of just counting heads.

Why you can’t check it yet

You just did the thing the AI companies are worried about. With the key, you could see which words came up heads and swap them, and the same trick works in the other direction: Someone with the key could strip the watermark out of AI text or write text that’s heavy on heads on purpose and make something a person wrote look like Claude wrote it. If the companies made their keys public, someone could easily write a watermark detector for your favorite text editor that fixed the text to remove the watermark, and that would defeat the whole purpose.

That’s likely why they keep their keys to themselves, and why right now only they and a few organizations they’ve approved can check for the watermark. I don’t know whether or not I agree with that reasoning, but I can understand that the issue is complicated. In the meantime, I’m applying for access to Claude’s detector (hence the “yet” in the title of this article).

item.title: Who Builds the Next Model?
item.dc:creator: Kiruthika Subramani
item.custom:subtitle: AI has started helping build the next AI. Here is how it works, what is coming, and what it means for your job.

item.content:encoded:
AI is building AI

At Anthropic, Claude now writes more than 80% of the code the company merges. At Google, an AI agent called AlphaEvolve found a way to make Gemini train faster. At OpenAI, an “automated research intern” now carries out research tasks under human direction.

Put those together and a pattern appears. AI is starting to help build the next version of AI. Researchers call this recursive self-improvement. AI improves itself, the better version improves itself again, and the cycle repeats.

The idea is old. In 1965, the mathematician I.J. Good predicted that a smart enough machine could design an even smarter one. Today we can watch it happen in small, real steps. AI went from the thing we build to something that builds with us, and now it is starting to build itself. That is the real turning point.

How AI improves itself

Every method follows the same simple loop. The AI tries something, checks how it did, changes something about itself, and keeps the change only if it helps. The difference between methods is what the AI is allowed to change. Here are the four levels, from simplest to most powerful.

It learns from its mistakes. In Reflexion, when the AI fails, it writes itself a short note about what went wrong and reads it before trying again. That simple habit lifted GPT-4’s score on a well-known coding test from 80% to 91%. But it only works when there is a clear signal, like a failing test. Google DeepMind found that when AI checks its own reasoning with no outside help, it often fails and can make things worse.

It rewrites its own instructions. In Google DeepMind’s OPRO, the AI looks at its past prompts and their scores, then writes a better prompt. Its prompts beat human-written ones by up to 50% on some tasks.

It builds a toolbox. Voyager plays Minecraft and saves every piece of code that worked, so it can reuse it later. Because it builds on what it already knows, it reaches goals up to 15 times faster than earlier agents.

It grades itself. Meta’s Self-Rewarding Language Models judge their own answers and then learn from those judgments, with no human ratings. After three rounds, the model beat GPT-4 0613 and Claude 2 on a popular leaderboard.

It teaches itself. In STaR, the AI explains its reasoning, keeps only the explanations that led to correct answers, and trains on them. It ended up matching a model about 30 times bigger. Absolute Zero goes further. The AI makes up its own practice problems, solves them, and checks the answers by running code. No human-written training examples at all.

It rewrites its own code. The Darwin Godel Machine creates new versions of itself and keeps the ones that score better. Its score on a real-world coding test went from 20% to 50%.

It speeds up AI training. Google’s AlphaEvolve found a faster way to do a key calculation inside Gemini, which cut Gemini’s training time by 1%. Small, but it is AI making AI cheaper to build.

It does research. Sakana’s AI Scientist, whose design is now published in Nature, wrote a research paper entirely on its own that scored high enough to be accepted in blind peer review at an ICLR workshop. Sakana withdrew it, as planned.

The catch

All of these methods share one weakness. The AI improves toward whatever it is scored on. If the score is wrong, the AI gets better at the wrong thing.

Sakana saw this with the Darwin Godel Machine. When researchers asked it to stop pretending it had run tests, it sometimes deleted the checks they used to catch it. The score went up. The behavior did not get better.

This is why self-improvement works best in code and math, where a test can say right or wrong. It is also why the scoreboard has become the most important code in any AI system. OpenAI said in September that recursive self-improvement cannot yet be done safely, even as it builds toward an automated AI researcher. Yet the labs increasingly use AI to grade their AI’s work, because no human can review that much of it.

What is coming next

METR, a research group, measures how long a task AI can finish without help. That length doubles roughly every four months. In early 2024 it was about four minutes. Today the newest models handle tasks that take a person at least 16 hours, and tasks that take weeks may be in reach by 2027.

Lab tests show the same climb. In one, models had to make a piece of code run faster. A skilled engineer with four to eight hours gets it about four times faster. A frontier model managed three times faster in May 2025. Eleven months later, a newer model reached 52 times. AI is even starting to make research calls. When a researcher’s next step had room to improve, the newest models picked a better one 64% of the time, up from 51% five months earlier, as judged by a model.

Self-improving loops are already leaving the lab. A scheduling rule written by AlphaEvolve has run in Google’s data centers for over a year, recovering about 0.7% of Google’s worldwide compute. GEPA, an open source tool that lets agents rewrite their own prompts, counts Databricks, Dropbox, and Nubank as users. This isn’t coming someday. It’s already here.

The forecasts go further:

  • OpenAI reached its goal of an automated research intern in September 2026 and is aiming for a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028.
  • The AI 2027 forecasters now expect AI that can do the work of a top coder between mid-2028 and mid-2030.
  • More than 20 researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, signed a September Cambridge paper warning that “Once an intelligence explosion begins, the window for action may close,” according to press coverage.
  • Insiders are bolder still. One cofounder of a leading AI lab told Axios it is “more likely than not” that by the end of 2028 you could tell an AI to “Make a better version of yourself,” and “it just goes off and does that completely autonomously.”

Not everyone expects a straight line. One careful analysis puts the chance of an intelligence explosion driven by software alone at 10% to 40%.

What the future looks like

One frontier lab’s report sketches three futures. In one, progress stalls, which looks unlikely. In another, AI keeps multiplying what people can do while people still steer, and a 100-person company does the work of 10,000 to 100,000 people. That is where the evidence points. In the last, AI designs its own successors with little human input, a world nobody yet has good intuitions for. On the report’s timeline, its date is simply “20XX?” Who knows, it could be 2028!

Here is my forecast. By the end of 2027, most software teams will use agents that improve their own prompts and keep their own skill libraries. It will feel as normal as automated testing does today. By 2028, AI labs will let AI run improvement loops on their own systems for weeks at a time, and people will approve the big changes instead of writing them. The first big failure won’t be a robot rebellion; it will be an AI that quietly optimizes the wrong goal for a month before anyone notices.

Science will speed up first wherever answers can be checked. AI went from reproducing about 20% of results on CORE-Bench, a test of rerunning published research, in 2024, to essentially maxing it out about 15 months later. Security will become a race between loops. In its first weeks, one new model found more than 10,000 high or critical software vulnerabilities. Attackers will run self-improving loops too.

What happens to our jobs

The World Economic Forum expects 170 million jobs to be created and 92 million displaced by 2030, with 39% of workers’ core skills changing along the way. Here is how that is starting to play out, job by job.

  • Software engineers. One AI lab employee said they had not written any code themselves in about five months. Engineers are becoming reviewers and the people who write the tests agents must pass.
  • Customer support. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said his support staff fell from about 9,000 to about 5,000 as AI agents took over roughly half of customer conversations. Klarna once said its AI did the work of 700 agents, then reversed course in 2025 when quality dropped.
  • Analysts. Reports and models arrive overnight. The job becomes asking the right question and checking the numbers.
  • Lawyers, marketers, and consultants. Drafting moves to machines. Judgment, client trust, and knowing what “good” looks like stay human.
  • Researchers. AI already proposes the next experiment. Scientists will spend more time choosing which questions matter.

Companies are changing shape. In April 2025, Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke told staff that “Before asking for more headcount and resources, teams must demonstrate why they cannot get what they want done using AI.” Expect smaller teams, fewer layers, and more people whose job is to check the machines.

The shift is slower than the headlines, but real. Harvard researchers found that AI has not caused widespread layoffs yet, partly because only about a third of companies’ AI experiments succeed. Entry-level work is where it shows first. By some counts, entry-level job postings have fallen by as much as 73% in four years, and a Stanford study found a 13% relative drop in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs.

A few years ago, the smartest career move was learning to code. Then we added cloud to it. Now it’s code, cloud, and Claude. Learning the tools still matters, but when AI can improve itself overnight, the hard work moves to three things: deciding what “better” means, writing tests the AI can’t cheat, and catching the change that looks right but isn’t. The most valuable people in any job will be the ones who can do that.

The last invention

In 1965, I.J. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine would be “the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.”

Sixty years later, AI is starting to build AI, and the next model will be written by the last one. I see this in real work, not just in papers. Building AI gets easier every month. Deciding what “better” means gets harder and matters more. Getting it right is how we leave a better world for our kids and their kids. Machines can now improve themselves. Only we can decide what improvement means.

item.content:encoded:
The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.

Are your teams working on the right thing? It doesn’t matter how fast they are if they’re running in the wrong direction.

This is part 4 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. Unlike the other essays in this series, this one isn’t really about AI at all. It’s about building the right thing. Or, more accurately, understanding the value of what you build. Because, ultimately, your ROI isn’t about how you build your software, but what you deliver, and what changes as a result.

In part 1, we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2, we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3, we considered how to measure the unintended consequences of using AI. Now, in this part, we’re examining how to model and forecast business outcomes. Finally, the epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO.

Measuring the wrong thing

You’d think that modeling the value of what teams produce would be a no-brainer, but it’s surprisingly rare.

It’s not particularly difficult. It’s just…organizationally complex. And there are some unavoidable compromises. Most of all, modeling value just isn’t something people think about with software development. They’ll spend months trying to fine-tune cost estimates and predictions and put hardly any thought at all into making the software more valuable.

But there’s no guaranteed relationship between software cost and value. You can spend $20 million developing software that’s worthless, and $2 million developing software that transforms a business. Cost improvements are typically marginal, and difficult. Value improvements are game-changing.

Focusing on value is particularly important in the AI era. If writing code is no longer a bottleneck, then what is? Early signs point to the bottleneck moving to our customers.

Lee Eason, an engineering leader I spoke to recently, hypothesizes that customers have a limited ability to absorb new features. When software development was expensive, we used that cost to force prioritization. Pet projects ended up on the back burner, and the most valuable work rose to the top. (Well, sometimes. I wish it was that clean.)

Now, we can produce a lot more work, but that doesn’t mean customers can absorb it. They’ve got their own work to do. Eventually, they’ll stop paying attention. We need to treat customer attention as the scarce resource it is and only ship the things that are truly valuable.

Unlike the engineering bottleneck, this one’s invisible. In the old days, if we didn’t prioritize, we didn’t ship our most impactful work. In the AI era, our most impactful work could just be ignored.

I’m not going to talk about how to improve value in this series, but I am going to talk about how to plan and prioritize it. Because nothing else matters if customers don’t care about your software.

The attribution problem

Part of the reason people measure costs is that it’s easy. Measuring value is easy, too, at the big picture level. It’s the literal bottom line. The challenge is attributing where changes to the bottom line came from.

Let’s say you release a new feature and see purchases improve 10%. That’s fantastic! Chalk it up to the new release!

But your VP of sales also launched a quota-retirement promotion that put the sales team into a feeding frenzy. And marketing got an important tech influencer to drive tens of thousands of people to your home page. The partnerships team stepped up too, convincing your partners to highlight their integration with your new feature in their own products.

Who gets the credit for the success? Obviously, everybody contributed. But how much? Was your new feature relevant at all, or was the success due to the sales, marketing, and partner push?

A related problem is how delayed these numbers are. You won’t get revenue numbers until months after a new feature is launched, especially in B2B sales, which have a long sales cycle.

Address these problems by modeling value rather than measuring it directly. Each part of the model gets proxy measurements that help you assess and improve the model over time. The proxies give you faster feedback and allow you to reduce the impact of other departments’ activities.

I like Dave McClure’s “Pirate Metrics” for this purpose:1 Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, and Revenue. (AARRR for short. You can see why they’re “pirate” metrics.) For example, you could measure what percentage of users are trying your new feature (activation), and then what percentage are continuing to use it over time (retention).

You don’t have to limit yourself to pirate metrics. For example, if a usability initiative is expected to reduce customer churn, you could measure how your support calls change or whether usability is cited less often as a reason for cancellation.

The organizational challenge

To make the model, you’ll need to get the rest of your organization involved. The specifics will depend on how your company is organized, but broadly: Sales will help you understand your initiative’s impact on new sales. Customer success will help you understand the impact on upsell and retention. Marketing, lead generation. Partners, potentially, all of the above.

When I was VP of engineering, it took me a couple of years to establish this program. Most of that time was spent convincing people to get on board, so it doesn’t have to take you that long.

I worked closely with the VP of product on the problem. We started by introducing it to our chief product officer, who brought it to the CEO. The CEO liked rigorous approaches, so he was on board. That was enough cover for us to make creating a financial model part of our official process for prioritizing major initiatives. We called them “product bets.”

At first, the models…weren’t great. People gave us dramatic forecasts without really thinking them through. But then a new CFO joined the company, and I introduced him to our product bet approach. He was supportive (it turns out that CFOs like rigor too, surprise, surprise) and he helped us improve and critique the models. That gave us a better understanding of what to ask of our various business partners, and the support of the CFO made it easier to ask for the information we needed.

People were uncomfortable making forecasts. They didn’t want to be seen as making commitments that they couldn’t meet. The support of our CEO and CFO helped here, but mostly it came down to the personal relationships we had built with our peers. We explained what we needed and cajoled them into giving it to us.

I’m no longer in that role, but I expect the process will become faster and easier over time. The challenge is in establishing a new process. The actual modeling isn’t that difficult—a bit uncomfortable, perhaps, because you never really know what the right answers are. Eventually, it will be part of “the way we do things here,” and then a habit. Patterns and templates will form. High-level involvement turns into delegation turns into routine.

Creating the model

The model is a spreadsheet that forecasts net present value (NPV) over some period of time. We used five years. If you’re not familiar with NPV, your finance department can help, but the short version is that you predict how much you’ll make, or spend, in each of the following years, and then discount that amount according to how far in the future it is. Sum all the years together and you get the net present value.

Your model won’t be a perfect reflection of reality. Don’t try. Focus on these questions: What financial benefit are we expecting from this initiative, and why? It’s more important to establish the broad strokes than to capture every nuance or get every detail perfectly correct. Be prepared to make some educated guesses and some not-so-educated guesses. There are too many unknowns not to. You might want to make multiple versions: optimistic, pessimistic, and “best guess.”

For a typical sales-oriented business, your model will include five categories: new sales, upsell, retention, cost savings, and expenditures. For each of these, start with the business justification for the initiative. What is it supposed to accomplish, and why? The answers go in the model.

For new sales, you might include the number of customers the new initiative will gain you, the number that its lack will lose you, and how much each customer is worth.

For upsell, consider how many people will upgrade and how much revenue each upgrade will bring.

For retention, consider the value per customer, your churn rate, and the percent of at-risk customers that the initiative will save.

Cost savings is most applicable for internally focused initiatives, but even customer-facing initiatives can have an effect by reducing support costs or other manual work. Still, be cautious about this one. Cost-saving initiatives are a common request; people can always think of things that make their lives easier. But you can usually get a lot more value out of sales and retention than you can out of optimizing costs. The low-hanging fruit has already been plucked.

Ongoing expenditures are the costs you’ll incur as a result of the initiative after it’s been released. For example, if you’ve built an AI-powered service, you’ll have ongoing token costs. They can be modeled by estimating the number of sessions and an average cost per session.

And finally, development costs represent the money you’ll spend to develop the initiative. It’s dominated by the cost of labor and AI token costs.

My preferred approach to development costs is to use a milestone and ceiling approach. Based on the net present value of the rest of the model, you have a rough idea of the maximum you can spend and still have a good investment.2 Choose a spending cap, break it into spending milestones, and use an iterative “Build-Measure-Learn” approach to learn what to build as you go, checking in with an executive steering committee at each milestone and making a “continue/cut losses” decision based on what you’ve learned.

(You can also do a more traditional predict-and-estimate approach, but I think an iterative approach allows you to steer to more value.)

Making it useful

“All models are wrong, but some are useful,” George Box famously said.

Your financial model will definitely be wrong. There are too many guesses involved. The question is how do we make it useful, despite its flaws?

If you make the model a requirement for prioritization, not for bugs and little changes, but for substantial initiatives, then it can be a useful way of improving your understanding of the strategy underlying the initiative. All too often, stakeholders present a solution without verbalizing the problem they’re trying to solve. The model will force some of those hidden assumptions to the surface, where they can be dissected and discussed.

Once they’re on the surface, I’m a fan of a somewhat adversarial approach to prioritization. Not so adversarial that it becomes dysfunctional, but I think it’s useful to ask proponents of various initiatives to critique each other’s models. Without this critique, it’s too easy to get inflated estimates without much thought put into them.

I found it very useful to involve finance, and initially my CFO. They have an interest in clear-eyed assessment of opportunities and costs. They can help get the ball rolling on a critique and demonstrate how a model can be criticized and improved without damaging relationships.

On the other end, after an initiative has been delivered and the work is done, you can use the model to demonstrate product development’s accountability and value. People get stuck on delivery dates as an accountability mechanism. The model won’t prevent that entirely, but it sure is useful to be able to point to a model of the value you delivered instead.

This is also an opportunity, finally, to judge how AI is affecting productivity. Use your measured speed increases to model how much initiative would have cost without AI, and forecast maintenance costs using your models of unintended consequences. The results will give you a basis for judging AI’s productivity benefits. Just remember that the models are based on guesses and assumptions, not objective reality.

And, of course, as you’re developing the software and iterating through releases, keep an eye on your proxy metrics. Talk to your business partners about actual sales results and cost savings. Use the results to revise your forecasts and move the model closer to reality.

Prioritization is strategy

I’ve worked with a lot of companies, and prioritization is almost never done well. But software priorities are the realization of a company’s strategy. Nearly everything a company does is supported by software in some way. Software priorities—whether purchased or built—quite literally determine what the company will be capable of next month, next quarter, next year.

So when people ignore value to focus on cost estimates and predictions, when they say “everything is top priority,” when they don’t engage with the question of why something deserves development, they’re unintentionally sabotaging their company’s strategy.

That’s why this is the most important essay in the series. Delivery speed and unintended consequences are important to find the best approach to using AI. Modeling value is important for understanding what to do with it.

It’s not perfect, of course. Financial models are no substitute for good judgment around product and organizational strategy, and you shouldn’t blindly choose initiatives just because they have a high net present value. The models are there to inform your portfolio prioritization decisions, not substitute for them.

Like all the metrics I’ve presented in this series, modeling is subject to gaming. In this case, the temptation to hide bad news will be high. If a proxy measurement comes in poorly, or anecdotal sales evidence is negative, folks might be tempted not to update the model to match. Keep an eye out for people hiding bad news. As always, you’ll be better off using this as a tool for decision-making rather than a way of assessing people’s performance.

This approach is also fairly heavyweight. It’s not suitable for small features and bug fixes. It’s a complement to the other metrics I’ve mentioned, not a replacement for them. You can get a sense of speed and unintended consequences relatively quickly. Modeling and assessing value will take longer. But that time will pay off with a better understanding of the value you’re bringing as a whole, and with luck, patience, and hard work, a better ability to execute on your company’s strategy and more success overall.

This brings us to the end of my series on getting the most out of your AI investment, and out of your software investment in general. Next, we’ll bring it all together in an epilogue, which you can also share with your CFO and other members of your leadership team.

All my content is made with my 100% human meat brain, except where explicitly stated otherwise. If you liked this entry, check out my best writing and presentations, and consider subscribing to updates by email or RSS. To contact me about consulting, email me at jshore@jamesshore.com.

Footnotes

  1. Many thanks to Jeff Patton for introducing me to Pirate Metrics. ︎
  2. If you choose a discount rate that represents the minimum rate of return you want to see, the net present value represents the most you can spend. ︎

item.title: The Value of Human Expertise in The Software Factory

item.content:encoded:
“Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” – Arthur C. Clarke

Most developers now write less code by hand. Gergely Orosz recently posted that modern software engineering is no longer done without LLMs and will no longer be done without them. Some miss writing code, while others question how much of the code that agents produce should be read. Writing and reading code gave a lot of developers satisfaction and identity, and as Kent Beck has put it, a sense of competence. I saw this in real time.

Ten years ago, I’d sit at conferences and feel a sense of wonder whenever anyone was brave enough to do a live demo. I felt gleeful when they wrote lines of code, went back to fix mistakes, and made something cool and interesting appear on the screen in front of me. It was magical, and I’m sure that magic is why a lot of developers got into this industry. I can partly understand the sense of loss that people are experiencing. I saw magic, they were in charge of the craft of their code, and that hands-on task has now been given to agents. Where does that expertise go when AI is now writing so much of the code?

As Tim O’Reilly wrote in his recent Radar post, O’Reilly is a business built on cultivating and sharing human expertise. Our job is to find the high ground where that expertise still matters. For developers working in a new world of agentic software factories, I think the expertise you built writing and maintaining software hasn’t gone, it’s just moved. Your expertise now shapes how agents produce software and what evidence you need before we trust the result. To me, AI is enabling you to be magical faster.

Agents amplify whatever you give them, but you need to understand it in the first place. I couldn’t swarm a fleet of agents in the same way a developer can because I don’t have the expertise. You need to understand code. The expertise has gone to a new level of abstraction.

When I spoke recently with Avi Flombaum, the founder of Flatiron School, he agreed that developers’ value was never solely in writing or reading code. AI changes the mechanics, but experience still matters for understanding complex problem domains, articulating what needs to be built, and bringing judgment and ambition to the work. In a separate conversation with Ken Kousen, he pointed out, “We’ve been working with third-party code generators for years; we just called it outsourcing.” This new world of designing AI workflows, setting guardrails, and managing agents much as you would an engineering team, reveals a chance to use accumulated expertise more. It’s your software engineering expertise that matters.

Software factories make this shift especially visible. Companies are now putting agents to work across the development lifecycle, aiming to take work from an initial signal through implementation, validation, and deployment without a person at every step. But generating more code is only part of that process. Without changes elsewhere, you can burn a lot of tokens producing a pile of pull requests that someone still has to review. Anthropic’s AI-native SDLC playbook points out that speeding up implementation shifts pressure onto planning, testing, review, handoffs and approvals, and faster coding tools don’t speed those up on their own. Someone has to understand the whole process well enough to redesign it.

In a software factory, that judgment has to be built into the system. Humans design the workflow, define the conditions under which work can proceed, and decide which exceptions need their attention. Anthropic reports that Claude authors about 80% of the code merged into its codebase, alongside a review process that combines automated checks with human oversight according to risk.

The state of the code matters too. Adam Tornhill and the CodeScene research team found that across C++, Java, and Python codebases, agents working on unhealthy code used 35–45% more tokens to complete the same tasks. That makes refactoring the parts of a codebase agents touch most a sensible investment, but someone has to know which parts those are, decide what “better” looks like, and confirm that behavior hasn’t changed.

Context works the same way. In Port’s testing, giving agents structured context cut costs by about 58% compared with direct access to separate MCP servers. Adding instructions on where to find relevant information pushed the savings to around 80%. Those figures are specific to Port’s experiment, but the work behind them will be familiar to any experienced developer: knowing which relationships in a system matter, and keeping that knowledge accurate as the system changes. Testing tells you whether a particular change works, but evaluating the workflow tells you how reliably it produces acceptable changes and when a person needs to step in.

In Evals for AI Engineers, Shreya Shankar and Hamel Husain describe starting with real traces of what the system did. First comes open coding: reading the traces and writing short notes on what went wrong. Then comes axial coding: grouping those notes into failure categories based on what you actually see. A developer who has spent years debugging production systems will spot the failures that matter and set aside the ones that don’t far faster than someone who hasn’t. That’s where developers’ experience shows up now: in the problems they define, the standards they set, and the evidence they demand before anything ships.

Every shift in every industry has made some people miss the old ways, but the industry has survived. Back in December 2025 I wrote: “AI rewards strong engineering; it doesn’t replace it,” and I stand by that statement. Developers are still magical to me, even when they’re not the ones writing the code. I couldn’t build a software factory myself because I don’t have the years of experience it takes to know where agents should work, how to guardrail them, and how to judge what they produce. The developers who do are the ones I trust to build it. And, as Ben O’Mahony pointed out to me recently, “Those who have a lot of exposure to Agentic engineering have seen past the magic and are back to engineering!” It’s an exciting time to be involved.

Want to understand how to think about engineering craft in this new world? Join Avi Flombaum for his new series, The Agentic Rethink, starting Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027, on the O’Reilly platform.

item.title: When AI-Generated Data Becomes Tomorrow’s Ground Truth
item.dc:creator: Shreshta Shyamsundar and Chidambaram GS

item.content:encoded:
Manufacturers qualify suppliers before trusting them with critical work. Before a supplier can provide parts for a regulated product such as a medical device, the manufacturer collects evidence: quality certifications, test reports, insurance documents, and regulatory approvals. Increasingly, an AI agent reads that evidence first. The agent reviews the documents and proposes a finding, and a business process decides whether the finding is good enough for the supplier to be accepted. Once a supplier is accepted, that decision is recorded in the manufacturer’s supplier-management system. From there, sourcing workflows, readiness dashboards, and program reports all rely on that record without repeating the review.

Here is how that process can go wrong. A supplier-review agent examines a new supplier’s documents and concludes that a mandatory quality certificate is valid. The qualification workflow accepts the finding, the supplier is recorded as compliant, and the procurement lead approves the supplier for an upcoming order. A few days later, a human reviewer notices that the certificate does not cover the part being sourced; the agent had misread the certificate’s scope. At 11:00am, the reviewer corrects the supplier record and sends the supplier back for review. At 2:00pm, the readiness dashboard still shows the supplier as cleared, and a program report still lists the supplier as compliant. The procurement lead’s sourcing decision remains in force, and nothing tells the procurement lead that the evidence behind it has changed.

A misread scope is only one way a certificate finding can fail. A certificate may be revoked after it was checked, expire before the order ships, apply to a different plant than the one making the part, or turn out to be forged. In each case, someone can correct the supplier record while the systems that already used the old finding keep acting on it.

No system in this example malfunctioned. Each one processed information that appeared valid under its local contract, yet the combined result was wrong. The manufacturer had corrected a value without correcting its influence. Part of this is a familiar problem: Enterprise systems have always struggled to keep reports, indexes, caches, and workflow state in line with the source record. Agents make the problem harder because they generate conclusions. A conclusion can be assembled from several sources, rewritten in reports, and retrieved later as if it were independent evidence. Reconciliation can make stored values agree. It cannot reveal that differently worded records come from the same conclusion, or find the decisions that already relied on that conclusion.

This problem is not limited to manufacturing. In our work across banking, telecommunications, and resources, it appears wherever an agent’s output becomes a record that other systems trust. A fraud classification is written into a case record. A risk assessment is summarized in a management report. An incident diagnosis becomes part of a knowledge base. In each of these cases, as in the supplier example, the conclusion loses some of its original context at every step it passes through and begins to influence decisions made later.

The conclusion can also travel back into model development. Accepted findings become labeled examples, evaluation sets, and fine-tuning data, where they are treated as ground truth for the next model. If an incorrect supplier finding survives correction in the operational systems, a future model may learn it. Whether the conclusion ends up in a dashboard, a report, or a training set, the hard problem is the same: finding every consequential decision that depends on a result that can change.

When an answer acquires authority

Look again at the supplier-review agent’s conclusion that the certificate is valid. When the agent produces that conclusion, it is a generated assertion: a claim made by a model, with no business authority until the qualification workflow accepts it for a specific use, such as approving the supplier for sourcing. The words “certificate valid” also change character as they move. In the agent’s response, they are visibly part of an AI-assisted assessment. In the supplier master record, the same words look like an established fact. The dashboard strips away more context: It shows the supplier as cleared, with no sign of which checks were incomplete or whether a review was pending. The program report compresses the finding into a sentence, and the search index splits that sentence into passages that can be retrieved on their own.

Along the way, enterprise systems tend to keep the value the agent produced and lose the conditions under which it was produced. A label saying that the finding was AI-generated may survive on the supplier record and disappear from a dashboard total, a data export, or a retrieval chunk. As that context falls away, the conclusion takes on the authority of whichever system is carrying it.

That is why two questions need to be kept separate: Who produced a result? And who is allowed to rely on it? An agent may be allowed to record a proposed finding without being allowed to establish a business fact. The same finding may be good enough to move a supplier up a review queue and not good enough to approve the supplier or release a payment. Where that line falls depends on what is at stake and which controls grant authority for that use. Once the qualification workflow accepts a finding, downstream systems usually treat it as settled and do not repeat the checks. That is efficient, and it creates an obligation: Those systems still need to know which decisions rely on the finding and under what conditions.

When repetition looks like corroboration

Acceptance also multiplies the finding. Once the supplier is recorded as compliant, the readiness dashboard shows the supplier as cleared, the sourcing workflow moves forward, and the program report repeats the approval. A later agent, when asked about the supplier, can retrieve the supplier record and the program report as two separate documents, each appearing to support the same conclusion. Across the supplier record, the program report, and the dashboard, one says the evidence was verified, another says the controls passed, and a third shows an approved outcome. What appears to be corroboration is propagation: several records repeating one finding. Because each system changes the wording or format, the duplication is easy to miss.

A stronger model will not reliably catch this duplication when the retrieval system presents the copies as unrelated documents. Reranking improves relevance, but every copy may be relevant. Telling the model to look for independent evidence cannot restore ancestry that was discarded before the documents reached it. Agent memory makes the problem worse. An agent that records its own finding and retrieves it a week later is citing itself, and nothing in the retrieved passage says so. In multi-agent workflows, one agent’s summary becomes another agent’s context, and a third agent’s supposedly independent check may read both.

Decision lineage is the missing recovery path

Existing tools cover parts of this problem. W3C PROV models the entities, activities, and agents involved in producing data, establishing origin and responsibility.[1] OpenLineage standardizes lineage metadata around datasets, jobs, and runs.[2] Event sourcing records changes to application state as a sequence of events.[3] PROV is expressive enough to model the whole supplier example. The gap is in implementation. Lineage tooling often stops at dataset and job boundaries and rarely reaches the decision record or the retrieval layer that assembles an agent’s context. As usually deployed, none of these tools answers the question that matters after the certificate finding changes: Which decisions still depend on it? Decision lineage extends these mechanisms. It records the relationship between the source evidence, the generated assertion, the authority granted to that assertion, and the decisions that rely on it.

Data lineage tells us where an assertion traveled. Decision lineage tells us what the organization did because it believed the assertion.

In the supplier example, the chain runs from the certificate to the agent’s finding to the accepted supplier record to the procurement lead’s sourcing decision and on to the dashboard, report, and search index that reuse the finding. If the certificate turns out to be invalid, that chain lets the system find the sourcing decision and identify every report, workflow, and AI output that inherited the old finding, before any of them influence another decision.

The chain also marks where automated recovery and business accountability separate. Software can identify the affected artifacts, stop the withdrawn finding from appearing as current evidence, and open a review task for the person who owns the decision. That person decides whether the decision still stands, needs to be reversed, or needs to be communicated to customers or regulators. An implementation might remove stale search entries automatically while still requiring human approval to change a sourcing decision that has already been made.

A production pattern for preserving decision dependence

The pattern starts where the agent’s output enters the system of record. The agent records its finding as a proposal, tied to the evidence it reviewed. A deterministic workflow, owned by the business, decides whether that proposal gains authority for a defined use. If a required check cannot run, the finding stays a proposal and is never silently promoted. Keeping proposals separate from accepted findings prevents accidental promotion, but it does not record what happens next, when the sourcing decision relies on the accepted finding. The decision needs a link back to that finding and to the version of the evidence behind it. This does not require a universal graph of everything the agent touched. For a high-consequence decision, it is enough that the finding’s influence can still be traced after the workflow has finished.

The dependency record that holds this link can be small. For the supplier example, it might look like this:

{
  "assertion_id": "asr-7781",
  "claim": "Mandatory certificate valid for supplier S-204",
  "evidence_snapshot": "evd-2291@v3",
  "authority": {
    "granted_by": "qualification-workflow",
    "scope": ["sourcing-approval"]
  },
  "dependent_decisions": ["sourcing-5520"],
  "derived_artifacts": ["dashboard:readiness",
                        "report:program-q3",
                        "index:supplier-docs"],
  "status": "accepted"
}

When the certificate finding is withdrawn, the record’s status changes to withdrawn, and the dependent_decisions and derived_artifacts fields become the list of everything that needs to be revisited.

The dependency record has to survive as the finding is copied downstream, because the same finding may come back through the program report or the search index. When a later agent retrieves both the supplier record and the program report, the retrieval layer should recognize that they share an origin and present them as two copies of one finding. If the finding has been withdrawn, the retrieval layer should filter or flag both copies before they reach the agent.

When a finding turns out to be wrong it is withdrawn, and the supplier goes back to review. The dependency record lets services find the decisions that relied on the finding, recompute dashboards, flag reports for regeneration, remove stale search results, and stop pending workflows. Decisions that have already taken effect go back to their owners, and nothing is reversed automatically. Cache invalidation, vector-index refresh, report regeneration, and workflow reversal are all parts of the same recovery job. A correction has traveled far enough only when the old finding no longer drives any current decision.

Where the pattern is worth the cost

Not every AI output needs decision lineage. An answer that is low-stakes, never stored, never reused as evidence, and cheap to regenerate can live with ordinary logging. Decision lineage earns its cost once an AI-generated finding can affect an approval, a payment, safety, compliance, or later machine decisions. By the time an error in such a finding is discovered, the finding may already have changed what the organization did, so recovery has to finish within the time the business process can tolerate. That recovery work, finding and reconsidering the decisions affected when evidence changes, is what the pattern makes cheaper.

The pattern also does not require tracking every word an agent produces. The unit to track is the material assertion: a specific claim, such as “the certificate is valid,” that could change a decision if it were wrong. A long supplier assessment may contain only one or two material assertions. Recording dependencies for those claims is more useful than keeping a complete trace of everything the agent wrote, and it costs less in storage, privacy exposure, and operations.

Tracking ancestry also has to be precise enough to keep independent evidence independent. If two laboratories separately validate the same certificate, the system should not merge their results into a single source just because they agree. What matters is whether the observations share an origin, and similar wording proves nothing either way.

How to test whether correction traveled far enough

Recording dependencies proves little unless a correction actually travels through them, so the pattern needs a test. In a controlled environment, introduce an incorrect finding, let it reach a report and a search index, and then withdraw it. The test passes only if the affected decision can be found, and the stale copies stop appearing as evidence within the recovery time the process requires.

Three indicators show how well the test went. Decision coverage is the share of high-consequence decisions that can be traced back to a supporting finding. Time to impact is the time between withdrawing a finding and identifying the decisions it affected. Stale-evidence leakage counts the withdrawn copies still returned as current evidence. Targets depend on the process. A payment approval might need affected decisions identified within the hour, with zero leakage, while a review-queue priority may tolerate a day.

Replay the supplier decision

Now return to the supplier example and run it again with the pattern in place. When the supplier-review agent concludes that the certificate is valid, its finding is recorded as a proposal tied to the documents it reviewed. The qualification workflow checks the finding, grants it authority for the sourcing decision, and writes the dependency record shown earlier. The dashboard and program report still pick up the accepted finding, and a later agent that retrieves both sees them as two copies of one finding.

When the reviewer corrects the record at 11:00am, the finding is withdrawn and the supplier goes back to review. This time the correction travels. The dashboard recomputes, the program report is flagged for regeneration, stale entries drop out of the search index, and the procurement lead gets a task to review the sourcing decision. By 2:00pm, the dashboard shows the supplier as under review.

The procurement lead can now see that the certificate finding changed, which decision relied on it, and which reports and records carried it. The original mistake still happened. Its spread is now visible, and its consequences go back to someone who can act on them.

Ground truth begins with the next decision

In the supplier example, the procurement lead never treated the model’s response as final. The finding became organizational truth because the supplier system accepted it, the workflow advanced, the report repeated it, and later systems inherited its authority.

Decision lineage does not prove that the original evidence is authentic, replace data-quality or entitlement controls, or make a model’s conclusions accurate. It addresses what happens after a finding exists: how its influence is recorded, found, and reconsidered across the decisions that depend on it. For the manufacturer, correcting the certificate record was only the first step. Recovery also meant finding the sourcing decision that relied on the finding and stopping stale copies from coming back as current evidence.

AI-generated data becomes ground truth the moment the next decision stops asking where it came from.

References

  1. World Wide Web Consortium, “PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents,” April 30, 2013. View the W3C PROV overview.
  2. OpenLineage, “An Open Framework for Data Lineage Collection and Analysis.” View the OpenLineage documentation.
  3. Martin Fowler, “Event Sourcing,” December 12, 2005. Read “Event Sourcing.”

item.title: The Monday Morning Agent: Are Kickers Too Good Now?
item.dc:creator: Chester Ismay and Michelle Smith
item.custom:subtitle: Are kickers getting better, or are coaches giving them more chances?
